grammar_help.title: Opening passive and proportion
grammar_help.text: Ymbseald means surrounded/beset; mid introduces the surrounding dangers. Efne reinforces the assertion. The paired swā clauses with comparatives mean the greater the worldly dignities, the fiercer the dangers. This proportional construction remains supported, distinct from prior equal-degree swā…swā.

grammar_help.title: Examples recognized and understood
grammar_help.text: Be ðǣm is a separate dative prepositional phrase, by/from that: it points back to the preceding proposition as the basis for inference. Bȳsena is the accusative examples governed by the two modal infinitives oncnāwan and ongietan. The paired verbs reinforce one act of understanding; do not treat bȳsena as dative because be appears earlier.

grammar_help.title: Tree, growth, result and reflexive
grammar_help.text: The relative ðe identifies the tree. Wiexð is the exact source third singular grows, beside the earlier selected wiext. The result clause ðæt hit hlīfað explains how it grows: so that it towers above the other trees. Brǣt hit means spreads itself; this hit is accusative and refers to the same tree. The first hit in the result clause is its nominative subject.

grammar_help.title: Storm and passive comparison
grammar_help.text: Sęmninga is suddenly. Gestęnt is singular present, assails/comes on; Cook’s note identifies storm and the following strong wind as its two subjects. Preserve the singular Old English wording; idiomatic English can use plural strike. The two following ðonne tokens function differently: then in the temporal correlation and than after swīðlicor more violently. Gewǣged and geswęnged are supplied passive bases. Se ōðer wudu means the rest of the forest, as the original note says.

grammar_help.title: Original157n3: hruron
grammar_help.text: Cook asks for the indicative preterite plural of hrēosan. Supply hruron (all plural persons); the classII plural uses u with s/r alternation. This is reference-only help, not a new complete productive hrēosan paradigm or an unaided recall task.

grammar_help.title: Cliffs and coordinated infinitives
grammar_help.text: Swā bið ēac gelīce be… means it is likewise also with/concerning…. The plural hīe refers to the cliffs/crags. Hlīfiað means tower and feorr ūp far up. Onginnað begin governs both feallan and hrēosan; full strengthens ðearlice, very violently. The two fall verbs can reinforce one collapse rather than name two chronologically separate events. Tō eorðan gives the destination to the earth.

grammar_help.title: ðā-ðe
grammar_help.text: Ðā-ðe is the exact joined source spelling of plural relative ðā with ðe, which. It is nominative plural as subject of standað and refers to muntum and dūnum. The prior compound-relative construction is reused with this explicitly supplied spelling; no new headword or unrestricted joining rule is inferred.

grammar_help.title: Mountains and punishment
grammar_help.text: Supply the repeated it is likewise with/concerning after Swilce ēac. Hēah is adverbial high with standað. Ðā-hwæðre means nevertheless. The mountains pay the penalty of their pre-eminence: the ðæt-clause explains that penalty. Geneahhe is often, preserving the source’s unmarked spelling beside dictionary genēahhe. Geðrēade, geðrǣste and geslægene are agreeing plural passive participles: punished/battered/struck by heavenly fire and thunderbolts. These exact forms do not assign three full new paradigms.

grammar_help.title: The human conclusion
grammar_help.text: The first subject is the high powers; hrēosað and feallað reinforce their fall, and weorðað tō lore means come to destruction. The second subject is the wealth of this world, which becomes sorrow (tō sorge). The third is these earthly wonders, which come to nothing (tō nāhte). The tō-result expressions are supplied; they are not instances of the earlier nominative-predicate become frame.
